Wingspan Bird Tier List

Wingspan Bird Tier List

This is a tier list of every bird in Wingspan's digital edition, including all the expansions and promo packs, ranked by a computer player. We built a computer player for Wingspan and had it play 510,000 three-player games against copies of itself. Then we looked at every bird a player drew blind off the deck and asked one question: did the players who got that bird end up further ahead than the players who got some other bird? The answer, in points, is the number under each card. Each tab is a separate list. Pick one, then tap a card for details.

The number is the bird's worth in points. It measures the change in your final lead over your best opponent (your score minus theirs) when you get this bird in place of an average one. Nobody chooses the top card of the deck, so across thousands of games everything else washes out and the difference belongs to the bird.

Values by round. Each bird has five values: one for the starting hand and one for each round. In these games the computer kept each starting bird on a coin flip, so luck decides which birds a player gets there too. White Stork is worth +8.9 points in the starting hand, +3.2 in round 2 and +0.9 in round 4. The number on the card blends the five, leaning on the early rounds because players gain more birds then. Tap a card for all five.

Based on 510,000 games, all played by the computer against copies of itself.

Surprises

  • The base game's famous "Power 4", Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer, all come out below average on the Oceania mats.
  • Point bombs rule. Of the 28 birds worth 8 or 9 points, all but one are at or above average, and they stay strong right through round 4.
  • Birds that draw bonus cards are the big winners. Four of the ten best birds in the game have that power, and seven in eight such birds are above average.
  • Wood Duck and Spangled Drongo are the best birds in the game to find in a starting hand, and worth little from round 2 on.
  • An extra turn is worth nearly 5 points, and every extra bird kept from the starting hand is worth about a point.

All birds

Click a column heading to sort by it. A bird's true value very likely lies within the margin of error on either side of the number shown.

Value
the bird's worth in points: the change in your final lead over your best opponent when you get this bird in place of an average one
Margin of error
the true value very likely lies this far either side of the number
Plays per 100 games
how often the computer played it, counting all three players
Forced play
now and then the computer was made to play a bird at random instead of the one it wanted. This is the average change in its final lead, in points, when the random pick was this bird. Near zero means it was about as good as the computer's choice, and a large negative number means the computer was right to pass it over
Usual round
the average round in which the computer played it
Points it scores when played
printed points plus the eggs, cached food and tucked cards on it at game end

The number is the bonus card's worth in points: the change in your final lead over your best opponent when you get this card in place of an average bonus card, measured in the same games and the same way as the birds. Bonus cards arrive blind too, dealt at the start or drawn by a bird's power, so the players who got a given card can be fairly compared with the players who got another. The value includes the choice of whether to keep the card, so a card the computer usually discards scores near zero at best.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.05 points, so cards a tenth of a point apart are effectively tied.
  • Kept when dealt is the share of the times the card was offered and the computer chose to keep it. Points when kept is the card's average score at game end.
  • A strong computer player's values. These come from the same 510,000 three-player games as the bird list, played by the computer player on the Oceania mats with nectar. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, but it plays well.

The computer player and the community tier lists

  • Wood Duck is as good as people say. Wingsplain's tier list puts Wood Duck in its top "God Tier", and Board Game Arena forum posters call it the strongest card outside the banned list and dead weight if drawn late. The computer agrees on all of it. Wood Duck is the third-best base-game bird and, with Spangled Drongo, the best bird in the game to find in a starting hand (worth +10 points there), and it is worth nothing in round 4. The computer also agrees with Wingsplain that Galah, Grey Butcherbird and Sacred Kingfisher are good Oceania birds, and that New Holland Honeyeater belongs near the bottom.
  • The "Power 4" are overrated. Common Raven, Chihuahuan Raven, Franklin's Gull and Killdeer top the King Panda Games base-game list and an R-bloggers card analysis, and Steam forum players call the Raven overpowered. On the Oceania mats, the computer rates all four below average, from −0.7 points for Franklin's Gull to −0.9 for Killdeer, and plays each of them less than once per 100 games. Once its printed points are set aside, Common Raven's power rates among the ten worst in the game. Nobody can promise the computer plays perfectly, and it learned only from games against copies of itself. But it is a strong player, and here the human consensus looks wrong for the Oceania game. All four turn your own eggs into food or cards, and that trade seems to have lost its value. Wingsplain's own notes call the Oceania game "egg-starved", and eggs make up only a ninth of the computer's score.
  • Many fan favorites are overrated. Maned Duck, Noisy Miner, Common Chiffchaff and Rainbow Lorikeet sit high on Wingsplain's list and below average on this one. Noisy Miner lands in the bottom tier even though the computer plays it often, and the computer almost never plays the other three. Base-game favorites from forum threads and top-10 articles, such as Spotted Towhee, Gray Catbird, Anna's Hummingbird and Green Heron, also land below average. These reputations come from the base game, and on the Oceania mats the birds look weaker than their fame.

Patterns across the whole deck

  • Point bombs are great. Of the 28 birds worth 8 or 9 points, all but one are at or above average, and they stay strong right through round 4. The exception, Scissor-Tailed Flycatcher, hands every player a food. Apart from the power, printed points are the most important thing on the card.
  • A bird's power is its most important quality. Points, egg limit, habitats, nest, wingspan and food cost together explain less than a fifth of the differences between birds. The power explains the rest. Among birds that are otherwise alike, each nectar in the cost takes away half a point. A bigger food cost is no drawback. An extra food in the cost goes with more value, about a quarter of a point.
  • Small egg limits are better. Birds with an egg limit of 0 or 1 average +0.7 points, and birds with a limit of 4 or more average −0.3. The gap holds among birds with the same printed points. Breeding Manager, the bonus card for big egg piles, is nearly the worst bonus card in the box, and Small Clutch Specialist, the bonus card for small egg limits, is a good one.
  • Birds that draw bonus cards are the big winners. Nine of the twenty best birds in the game have a power that draws bonus cards. Seven in eight such birds are above average, and they are worth more drawn in rounds 2 and 3 than in the starting hand. Fittingly, Endangered Species Protector, the bonus card for exactly these birds, is by far the best bonus card.
  • Nectar birds are weak. Nearly every bird with nectar in its cost is below average, and the computer almost never plays them. Spangled Drongo is the great exception, and with Wood Duck the best card in the game to find in a starting hand.
  • Promo birds are the strongest. The promo packs beat the base game and every expansion, even when comparing birds with the same printed points. The base game and the three expansions are about equal to one another. The New Zealand and Asia packs are the best, and the UK pack is the only weak one.
  • Eagles are strong. Every eagle in the game but Greater Spotted Eagle is above average, led by Steppe Eagle, Bonelli's Eagle and Philippine Eagle. Predators that look at the top card of the deck and tuck it if it is small come out a little above average on the whole, and predators that roll the dice for a fish or rodent are mostly below average.

Nearly identical birds

  • Extra habitats add value. Among birds with the same power, each extra habitat is worth about a quarter of a point, and some cases are far bigger. Chipping Sparrow (forest or grassland) beats Grasshopper, Baird's and Cassin's Sparrows (grassland only) by nearly 3 points with identical cost and power. Three-habitat House Finch likewise beats wetland-only Tree Swallow.
  • Among birds with the same power, more printed points help. Many base-game birds share "draw 2 new bonus cards and keep 1". All but 3-point Sprague's Pipit are above average, and the more points printed on the card, the better the bird, from King Rail near zero up to 8-point Atlantic Puffin at +3.9. Each extra printed point adds about half a point of value, and 4-point Bell's Vireo (+2.5) is the odd one out. White Stork, the second-best bird in the game, shares its power to refill the tray with two weaker birds, and its 8 points make the difference.
  • Tucking birds need a draw. Brown birds that tuck a card from your hand and draw a replacement are mostly above average. The ones with no draw are mostly below average, and three of them, Sulphur-Crested Cockatoo, European Golden Plover and Noisy Miner, are among the weakest cards in the game. Ruff, which draws a card for every card it tucks, is excellent.

Early birds and late birds

  • Pink birds are best in the starting hand. Pink birds are the strongest color at three players, but their value comes early. They are superb starting-hand cards and slightly below average by round 4. White birds climb from below average in the starting hand to solidly above average later. Yellow birds are the worst color to open with.
  • Some birds are only good early. Wood Duck, Spangled Drongo, Laughing Gull and Chipping Sparrow are among the best starting-hand cards in the game and worth nothing in round 4. The birds that get better late are white birds that draw bonus cards. North Island Brown Kiwi is the best bird to draw in round 4, with Atlantic Puffin, Giant Fish Owl and Steppe Eagle close behind.

Power families

  • "Play an additional bird" powers are weak. Not one bird whose power lets you play an additional bird at its normal cost is above average. Players prize the saved action, and the computer may underrate it, but at three players it rarely finds these birds worth playing. Yellow-Eyed Penguin is the lone exception at +3.9, and the difference seems to be the word "free".
  • "All players" powers hurt. Brown birds worth 6 points or more with a power that gives every player the same thing average about a point less than other brown birds with the same printed points, and the gift is the main reason some 7-point birds are bad. Cheap birds with the same kind of power are the worst cards in the game: six of the eight lowest birds, Rock Pigeon and Western Meadowlark among them, hand every player an egg, a food or a card. Giving to one chosen opponent hurts less than giving to everyone. At two players the cost should be smaller.
  • Free dice are gold. Pink birds that take a die from the birdfeeder on other players' turns are all above average, Eurasian Wren (+2.6) and Laughing Gull (+2.5) especially. Powers that give one named food from the supply are mostly below average, and none of the base-game jays and woodpeckers that take "1 seed from the birdfeeder, if available" is above average.
  • Spending food for points loses. Brown powers that spend food to tuck cards, lay eggs or draw cards are a losing trade, and every one of them sits below average. Caching for free works: every base-game chickadee and nuthatch that caches a seed from the supply is above average despite its small points.
  • Card draws pay early. Brown powers that draw several cards and let you keep one are excellent in the starting hand and below average from round 2 on. New Zealand Dabchick, Australian Ibis and Demoiselle Crane are the best of them. Powers that simply draw a card into your hand are all below average.
  • Round-end and game-end egg powers are weak. Teal and yellow birds that lay eggs are the weakest birds of their colors, and only Black Swan among the yellow egg-layers is above average. The "lay 1 egg on each of your birds" family is weak at every color, with Say's Phoebe (+0.9) the clear best of them.
  • Some powers go unplayed. Several whole families sit near the bottom because the computer almost never plays them: birds that move themselves to another habitat, most birds that copy another bird's brown power, and the teal birds that count double toward the end-of-round goal. Their low values mostly come from the computer declining to play them, and a player with a good bird to copy in view may do better with them. Birds played less than once per 100 games carry a grey "rarely played" flag in the list, and their order among themselves means little.
  • The raptors played on top are a special case. Red Kite, Eurasian Hobby, Montagu's Harrier and Common Buzzard, the European birds played on top of another bird, all sit in the bottom two tiers. The computer plays them about once per 100 games, and right after it does, it judges its own position more than a point worse. It seems to play them badly, so a player who picks the right bird to cover may get more from them.

Bird families

  • Cuckoos are excellent. The cuckoos and cowbirds that lay on another bird when a rival takes the lay-eggs action are nearly all above average, led by Common Cuckoo, Bronzed Cowbird and Violet Cuckoo. The computer plays them nearly twice as often as an average bird, and they are best drawn early and worth nothing from round 3 on.
  • Flightless birds are excellent. The kiwis and Yellow-Eyed Penguin are among the best cards in the game, and Takahē, Weka, Kākāpō and Little Penguin are well above average too. Emu and Southern Cassowary fall short.
  • Geese, herons and starlings disappoint. Geese and swans carry plenty of printed points and still come out ordinary, none better than Tundra Swan and Greater Snow Goose at +0.5. Herons and egrets are weak too, apart from Black-crowned Night-Heron. Starlings and mynas are below average except Common Starling and Bali Starling. Ducks are all over the place, from Wood Duck and Mandarin Duck near the top to Northern Shoveler and Pacific Black Duck near the bottom.

Nests, wingspans and food costs

  • Star nests are best. Birds whose nest counts as any type do clearly better than birds with a fixed nest, by about half a point among birds with the same printed points and egg limit. End-of-round goals and bonus cards keyed to nest types reward a nest that counts as all of them, though these birds may also simply have better powers.
  • Wingspan doesn't matter. Among birds with the same printed points, big and small birds come out the same, and all but one of the bonus cards keyed to wingspan are poor. Big wingspans simply come with big points.
  • Food type barely matters. Birds paid in rodents or fish do a little better than birds paid in invertebrates, and birds paid entirely in seed do a little worse, mostly because the computer rarely plays them. Wild food in the cost makes no difference, and the flexible "or" cost is no bargain.

Expansions, colors and habitats

  • A printed point is worth more in the expansions. Each extra printed point on a bird adds the least value in the base game and the most in the European expansion, about four times as much. The base game's big birds suffer most, for two reasons. Its birds with no power at all, such as Wild Turkey and Trumpeter Swan, trail powered birds of the same points by more than half a point, and its many brown "all players" birds are weak at nearly every point value.
  • European round-end birds are weak. The European expansion introduced the teal round-end power, and its own teal birds are the weakest version of it. Ruff, Common Goldeneye and Eurasian Collared-Dove are the exceptions. The Asian and promo teal birds do much better, led by Sri Lanka Blue-Magpie, the best bird in the game, with Tufted Puffin and Mandarin Duck behind it.
  • Brown grassland birds are the weakest. Brown birds that live only in grassland are the weakest habitat-and-color group in the game, and two in five of them are rarely played. Brown forest and wetland birds do better, and white grassland birds are fine. Nearly the only brown grassland birds that pay are predators such as Greater Roadrunner. The rest mostly lay or trade eggs, and egg powers lose value on the Oceania mats.

Timing and the tray

  • The starting hand matters most. Birds differ more than four times as much in value in the starting hand as in round 4. Keeping a dealt Spangled Drongo or Wood Duck instead of discarding it is worth more than 11 points, and keeping Spotted Dove, the worst opener, costs about 3.5. No bird drawn in round 4 costs even 1. So choosing which starting birds to keep is the decision to sweat over.
  • Printed points barely matter in the starting hand. Big and small birds are nearly even as starting-hand cards, and from round 2 on the number in the corner becomes the best single guide to a bird's value. Early, the power decides: pink birds and brown card-drawers are the best birds to keep from the starting hand.
  • Brown card-drawers fade. Brown birds that draw cards are excellent in the starting hand and slightly below average by round 4. Birds with "all players" powers are a real liability in the starting hand, since the gift to opponents adds up over a whole game, and harmless by round 4.
  • The tray is a bargain bin. Birds nobody wants sit face up until someone takes them, so three-fifths of the birds on offer in the tray come from the bottom half of this list. The computer picks accordingly. It takes an S-tier bird 84% of the time one is on offer and a C- or D-tier bird about 2% of the time. When a random move made it take a bottom-tier bird instead of its own pick, it finished about a point worse.
  • A strong bird in a rival's hand costs you half its value. When an opponent draws a bird, you finish about half the bird's value worse off against your best opponent (or better off, if the bird is weak). A rival's White Stork costs you 2.1 points. So taking a great bird from the tray also keeps it away from the next player.

Turns, actions and the opening

  • Keep birds over food. In these games the computer kept each starting bird on a coin flip, so the value of each kept bird shows directly. Every extra bird kept, with one less food, is worth about a point. Players who kept all five birds finished nearly 6 points better off than players who kept none. The first kept bird adds 1.7 points and the fifth only 0.5.
  • Keep invertebrates and seed. Against the average starting food, a kept invertebrate is worth +0.4 points and a seed +0.2. Fruit (−0.1) and fish (−0.1) are a shade below average, and rodent (−0.4) is the worst food to keep.
  • A turn is worth nearly 5 points. The Oceania "no goal" tile lets everyone keep that round's goal cube, so every later round has one more turn. With no goal in round 1, players scored 13 points more than average, from three extra turns and despite the missing goal. With no goal in round 4 there is no extra turn, and players scored 4.6 points less. Counting the goal points given up, each extra turn is worth nearly 5 points.
  • Playing a bird is the best action in every round. Now and then the computer had to take a random action. Against an average random action, playing a bird gained 0.4 to 1.1 points in every round. Drawing cards is good in round 1 (+0.6) and the worst action in round 4 (−1.3). Laying eggs runs the other way: the worst action in round 1 (−1.1) and the second best in round 4 (+0.7). The computer's own choice beat every one of these random actions, and a random action other than the one it wanted cost it 1.5 to 2.4 points.
  • Bird cards carry the score. The computer averages 108 points a game, and 49 of them come from the birds' printed points. Bonus cards bring about 14 points, eggs and end-of-round goals about 11 each, and tucked cards, nectar and cached food bring the rest.
  • The first player's edge is small. The first seat wins 34.6% of three-player games and the third seat 31.7%, a gap worth about a point.

Random bird plays

  • The computer's picks are worth about a point. One time in fifty, the computer had to play a random bird from the ones it could afford. Against its own choice from the same kind of hand, a random play cost it about a point on a typical bird, and for about half the birds the random play did clearly worse. For no bird did the random play do clearly better.
  • Some birds are traps. When a random move made the computer play Crimson-Bellied Tragopan, European Serin, Horsfield's Bushlark or Common Chiffchaff, it did 5 to 10 points worse than with a random playable bird. The computer is right to pass them over.

Bonus cards

  • A bonus card is only as good as its birds. Bonus cards for strong groups of birds are strong, as with Diet Specialist (three-food birds), Small Clutch Specialist (egg limit of 2 or less) and Rodentologist. Bonus cards for weak groups are weak, as with Backyard Birder (low-point birds) and Bird Feeder (seed-eaters). Cartographer is the exception: its birds are ordinary, but a few birds with geography terms in their names already pay off.
  • Player-mat bonus cards hold up late. Bonus cards for a kind of bird lose value as the game goes on, since there is less time left to collect. Rodentologist falls from +0.7 points in the starting hand to +0.2 in round 4. Cards that score the shape of your player mat hold their value or gain, since they pay for a mat you already have. Mechanical Engineer and Ethologist are strong in the starting hand and in every round.
  • Bonus cards need about 4 points. A bonus card that won't reach about 4 points is a net loss. The worst ones pay for low-point birds, big egg piles, leftovers in hand or supply, or a row of birds in rising or falling order. Backyard Birder, Breeding Manager and Visionary Leader are the worst in the box, with Citizen Scientist, Winter Feeder and the Ranger cards close behind. Endangered Species Protector, Mechanical Engineer, Ethologist and Ecologist are the best.

Fine print

  • Small differences don't mean much. Each value is good to about ±0.14 points, so birds a few tenths apart are effectively tied. Splitting the games into two halves and rating the birds in each half separately gives nearly the same list. The two sets of values have a correlation of 0.99, where 1 would be a perfect match.
  • Tray picks are left out. The numbers come only from birds that arrive face down: drawn from the deck, by the draw-cards action or by a bird's power, or dealt into the starting hand. A bird taken from the tray is a choice, so the players who take it aren't a fair comparison. The same goes for a card picked from several drawn by a power. Most cards arrive blind anyway: 91% of the bird cards that reached a hand came straight off the deck.
  • Each game result is compared with a forecast. Throughout a game, the computer keeps an estimate of each player's final lead or deficit against their best opponent. A bird is judged by the gap between the real result and that estimate as it stood just before the bird came off the deck. The estimate is made before anyone sees the card, so it can't favor any bird, and it stops a player who was already far ahead from making the card they happened to draw look good.
  • A strong computer player's values. These come from 510,000 three-player games of the computer player against copies of itself. It learned the game on its own, with no strategy advice from people. Nobody can promise it plays perfectly, but it plays well, and its disagreements with popular opinion (more on those above) deserve a hearing. In these games it also kept its starting birds on a coin flip, made one tray pick in five at random, and one time in fifty took a random action or played a random bird, so it played a little below its usual level. Those random moves are the source of several findings above.
  • Three-player games on the Oceania mats with nectar. Birds whose worth depends on the number of opponents, pink powers for example, could rank differently at two or four players.
  • Every bird is here. All 586 birds of the digital edition are in the list.
  • Tap any card for a larger view, its value and margin of error, its value in the starting hand and in each round, and the rounds the computer tends to play it in.
